title: Verifier‑Assisted versus One‑Shot LLM Intent→Configuration: A Paired NetOpsTraceBench Study (Revision: topology‑cluster disclosure)
abstract: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, a paired comparison of a one‑shot LLM intent→configuration pipeline and a verifier‑assisted generate–validate–repair pipeline on 1,200 intent→config episodes. Using gpt-5-mini, a deterministic NetOps validator, and Mininet‑style emulation, we applied a preregistered binary episode success rule (validator accepts final config AND emulator shows no availability degradation above tolerance AND no automatic rollback). Of 1,200 planned paired tasks we completed 1,199 pairs. Baseline success = 1,196/1,199 (0.9974979149); guarded success = 1,199/1,199 (1.0000000000). The paired‑success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0025020851 (95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.0000, 0.0058381985], bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25. The preregistered minimum detectable effect (5 percentage points) was not met given the observed near‑ceiling baseline; repair was invoked only three times. Crucially, the preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory breakdown (H3) was not executed for this run; the archived confirmatory analysis contains only pooled results (see analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/results.json). We provide artifact references and an explicit methodological note explaining the shared_initial_candidate paired design and its implications for repair invocation and external validity.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent expressed in natural language into executable device configurations for network operations (NetOps). Prior surveys and system papers emphasize that operational correctness depends on the orchestration stack (model + verifier + provenance + sandboxed execution) rather than the base LLM alone [1,2]. Generate–validate–repair (verifier‑assisted) architectures are a canonical mitigation: an LLM proposes candidate outputs, an automated verifier checks constraints and safety, and a repair loop iterates until verifier rules are satisfied [3–5]. However, publicly archived, preregistered, paired evidence measuring whether verifier assistance yields an operationally meaningful improvement (rollback‑aware binary success) relative to one‑shot generation is scarce.

We designed NetOpsTraceBench to address this gap. The preregistered study (ID rX4f7-1) compared two paired conditions per task (shared initial candidate): (A) baseline one‑shot NL→config generation and (B) a guarded generate–validate–repair pipeline. Our primary confirmatory estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Contributions: (1) a preregistered experimental design and complete execution artifacts; (2) a paired analysis on 1,199 completed pairs using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator; (3) transparent reporting that the preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory hypothesis (H3) was not executed and that the archived analysis contains only pooled results, together with artifact pointers supporting reproducibility.
sections.related_work: Surveys and system proposals frame LLMs as components of broader AIOps/NetOps workflows and repeatedly emphasize that correctness and trustworthiness are properties of the whole orchestration stack [1–3]. Prior work demonstrates generator+verifier loops for NL→formal translations, topology compilation, and domain‑specific configuration repair; reported gains depend on dataset selection and verifier strictness [4–10]. Empirical studies of LLM failure modes—hallucination, unit/semantic errors, overconfidence, provenance loss, and prompt‑injection—motivate guarded architectures but also highlight sensitivity to evaluation design [11–14]. Recent calls for workflow‑centered benchmarks (trace quality, validator interactions, emulator execution, preregistration) directly motivated NetOpsTraceBench [1,2]. Our study differs by preregistering a paired, rollback‑aware binary success rule and archiving provider/validator traces and analysis artifacts to permit exact replay.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory plan: The study preregistration (rX4f7-1; preregistration manifest SHA‑256 = 77abe8b493bde44484e0b3d02cfd7f9ec1621ff7e7847889082ae177a7ed5712) froze hypotheses (H1–H3), inclusion/exclusion rules, seeds, stopping rules, and the analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). The primary hypothesis (H1) tests whether paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline > 0 at α=0.05. H3 preregistered an exploratory confirmatory breakdown by topology cluster (edge vs core). Important revision disclosure (response to peer review): H3 was preregistered but was not executed in the archived confirmatory analysis; the archived confirmatory artifacts contain only the pooled paired analysis. The pooled artifacts demonstrating the primary result are analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json, analysis/missingness_summary.csv, and execution/execution_manifest.json. No per‑cluster confirmatory contingency files are present in the archived analysis artifacts for this run.

Task corpus and execution contract: The benchmark consisted of 1,200 deterministically generated tasks (edge=600, core=600) produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 using frozen per‑task seeds. Each task embeds structured fields (initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, workflow_policies) and a declared difficulty. Contamination detection and deterministic exclusions were preregistered (token/subsequence threshold T_contam=0.85; optional embedding similarity checks). Adapter orchestration used hosted_netops_gvr_v1; requested_model = gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applied the scoring rule "full_intent_constraint_validation". Generation semantics were shared_initial_candidate: baseline and guarded episodes used the same initial candidate per pair to isolate verifier/repair effects. Per preregistration: initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1 and maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; repair calls are conditional and logged.

Primary metric and analysis: The preregistered binary episode success requires (1) validator acceptance of the final configuration (validation_after.valid == true), (2) emulator execution with no availability degradation above tolerance, and (3) no automatic rollback during execution. The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The archived confirmatory analysis executed an exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary outcomes (n10, n01) and computed a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000) as recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl; analysis/results.json contains the reported estimate, p‑value, and CI.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting: The run completed 2,398 of 2,400 planned episodes, yielding complete_pair_count = 1,199 (failed_episode_count = 2; missingness summary in analysis/missingness_summary.csv). Provider audit: hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,203; completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,202; failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 1; stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 1,200, repair = 3 (execution/execution_manifest.json; deterministic_reconciliation.json).

Primary pooled outcomes (archived pooled artifacts): The pooled 2×2 contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 1,196, n10 = 3, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Baseline_success_rate = 1,196/1,199 = 0.9974979149; guarded_success_rate = 1,199/1,199 = 1.0; paired difference = 0.0025020851. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0000, 0.0058381985] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). All the numbers above are present in analysis/condition_summary.csv and analysis/results.json.

Topology‑cluster confirmatory breakdown (H3): As noted above, H3 was preregistered but was not executed in the archived confirmatory analysis for this run. The archived confirmatory artifacts contain only the pooled contingency table and pooled inferential outputs (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/results.json). No per‑cluster contingency CSVs or per‑cluster confirmatory result JSONs are present in the archived analysis bundle for this execution. Therefore no pooled‑to‑cluster inferential claims are made; any per‑cluster comparisons would require reanalysis not present in the archived confirmatory artifacts and are left as follow‑up work.

Repair diagnostics and interpretation anchors: Repair was invoked three times (stage_counts.repair = 3), matching repair provider traces in execution/provider_calls. Representative scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json, execution/scoring/task-000002-*.json, execution/scoring/task-000003-*.json) show validation_after.valid = true and repair_applied = false for the majority of episodes, indicating that the shared initial candidate often satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 checks. The small number of discordant pairs (3 favoring guarded, 0 favoring baseline) explains the non‑significant McNemar p and the bootstrap CI including zero.
sections.discussion:
Statistical and operational interpretation: The pooled analysis shows no statistically significant advantage for the guarded pipeline under the supplied corpus and validator configuration (p = 0.25; CI includes zero). Two artifact‑grounded operational explanations are evident in archived traces. First, near‑ceiling baseline performance (≈99.75%) leaves little absolute headroom; the preregistered MDE (5 percentage points) assumed a much lower baseline and thus the run was not powered to detect the observed ≈0.25 percentage‑point gain. Second, the shared_initial_candidate paired design and the deterministic task generator/validator combination materially reduced repair invocation: a single initial candidate per task was used and validator acceptance was common; repair was therefore rarely exercised (repair = 3). These interpretations are supported by execution/execution_manifest.json, deterministic_reconciliation.json, and representative scoring artifacts.

Methodological note on shared_initial_candidate design: We used shared_initial_candidate semantics (both conditions receive the identical initial LLM candidate) to isolate verifier and repair effects from generation variance. That choice reduces generation noise but also reduces opportunities for the guarded pipeline to improve over baseline when the initial candidate already satisfies verifier rules. In practice, this design clarifies the incremental value of verifier‑guided repair conditional on the same generator output, but it can produce small measured gains when initial candidates are already valid; artifacts (stage_counts and scoring traces) confirm this mechanism for the present run.

Threats to validity and externality: Internal validity is supported by frozen seeds, deterministic task generation, and automated exclusion rules. Construct validity concerns whether the binary success rule maps to broader operational correctness in production. External validity is limited: only one model family (gpt-5-mini) was exercised, tasks are synthetic/consented and vendor‑agnostic, and emulation may miss production idiosyncrasies (routing convergence, vendor renderers). Conclusion validity: very low discordant counts constrain statistical resolution for small absolute differences. These limitations are enumerated explicitly in the Limitations section and in the archived preregistration.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, producing a pooled paired comparison on 1,199 complete pairs. Under the supplied synthetic task corpus, deterministic validator settings, and requested_model = gpt-5-mini, baseline one‑shot generation attained near‑ceiling success (≈99.75%), the guarded pipeline yielded a small absolute increase (~0.25 percentage points), and the pooled exact McNemar test was not significant (p = 0.25; 95% CI includes zero). Importantly, the preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory hypothesis (H3) was not executed for this run; the archived confirmatory artifacts contain only pooled results (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/results.json). The run artifacts and logs (execution/execution_manifest.json, deterministic_reconciliation.json, analysis/*) are archived to enable reproducible follow‑up studies that vary task adversariality, verifier strictness, model family, and whether per‑cluster confirmatory analyses are performed.

limitations: Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across other LLMs or fine‑tuned variants.
Task corpus skew: synthetic/consented tasks yielded near‑ceiling baseline success (≈99.75%), limiting headroom and statistical power to detect practical improvements by guarded pipelines.

Emulator fidelity: Mininet‑style emulation and deterministic validators approximate production behavior but may not capture all deployment failure modes (routing convergence, vendor idiosyncrasies, transient telemetry).

Verifier configuration dependence: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 acceptance thresholds and parsing rules materially affect outcomes; different verifier strictness could change repair invocation rates and measured gains.

Analytic deviation documented: the preregistration specified a Wilcoxon signed‑rank paired procedure; the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar test because outcomes were binary. This deviation is recorded in analysis/results.json and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl.
Operational external validity: absence of heterogeneous vendor renderers, real production templates, and live rollouts constrain direct production generalization.
